CourseName: CEN3722 - Introduction to Human Computer Interfaces

Outcomes.Text: Explain the purpose and structure of WCAG guidelines and their role in inclusive interface design.
Identify accessibility gaps in existing prototypes through systematic auditing techniques.
Apply accessible color contrast ratios and visual design principles to interface components.
Demonstrate keyboard navigation patterns that support users who do not rely on a mouse.
Evaluate screen reader compatibility of interface elements using semantic markup and ARIA roles.
Create corrective design patterns that address identified accessibility failures in prototypes.

Topics.Title: Foundations of WCAG Guidelines
Topics.Summary: This topic introduces the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, their organizational structure, and why they serve as the authoritative standard for accessible digital design.

Elements.Title: What WCAG Is and Why It Matters
Elements.BodyText: WCAG is an internationally recognized set of guidelines published by the W3C that defines how to make web and interface content accessible to people with disabilities.
Elements.Notes: Emphasize that WCAG is not just a legal compliance checklist but a design quality framework. Many regions have adopted WCAG as the legal baseline, including the EU Accessibility Act and Section 508 in the US.

Items.Text: WCAG stands for Web Content Accessibility Guidelines and is maintained by the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C).
The guidelines address a broad spectrum of disabilities including visual, auditory, motor, and cognitive impairments.
Adherence to WCAG reduces legal risk and broadens audience reach for digital products.

Elements.Title: WCAG Conformance Levels: A, AA, and AAA
Elements.BodyText: WCAG organizes its success criteria into three conformance levels that indicate the degree of accessibility support provided by an interface.
Elements.Notes: Level AA is the most commonly required standard for commercial and government products. Level AAA is aspirational and not always feasible for all content types.

Items.Text: Level A represents the minimum accessibility threshold and addresses the most critical barriers.
Level AA is the widely adopted industry and legal standard targeted by most organizations.
Level AAA offers the highest degree of accessibility but is not required for all content.

Elements.Title: The Four POUR Principles
Elements.BodyText: WCAG is built on four foundational principles — Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, and Robust — that together define what it means for content to be accessible.
Elements.Notes: Use the POUR acronym as a memorable scaffold. Each principle maps to a category of user need: perception relates to sensory access, operability to motor access, understandability to cognitive access, and robustness to assistive technology compatibility.

Items.Text: Perceivable means all information must be presentable to users in ways they can sense.
Operable means all interface components and navigation must be usable regardless of input method.
Understandable means content and interface behavior must be predictable and clear.
Robust means content must be interpreted reliably by a wide variety of assistive technologies.

Elements.Title: Applying WCAG Success Criteria
Elements.BodyText: Each WCAG principle contains specific, testable success criteria that designers and developers use to evaluate whether an interface meets accessibility requirements.
Elements.Notes: Success criteria are the actionable, testable statements. Point students to the official WCAG quick reference at w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/quickref/ as a practical auditing tool.

Items.Text: Success criteria are written as pass/fail statements that can be objectively evaluated.
Each criterion is tied to a conformance level indicating its relative importance.
Designers should map their interface components to relevant criteria during the audit process.

Topics.Title: Accessible Color and Visual Design
Topics.Summary: This topic covers the principles and techniques for designing visual interfaces that are perceivable by users with low vision, color blindness, and other visual impairments.

Elements.Title: Color Contrast Ratios
Elements.BodyText: WCAG defines minimum contrast ratios between foreground text and background colors to ensure readability for users with low vision or color deficiencies.
Elements.Notes: The WCAG AA standard requires a 4.5:1 ratio for normal text and 3:1 for large text. AAA requires 7:1 and 4.5:1 respectively. Tools like the WebAIM Contrast Checker or Figma plugins can automate this check.

Items.Text: Normal text must achieve a minimum contrast ratio of 4.5:1 against its background at WCAG AA level.
Large text, defined as 18pt or 14pt bold, requires a minimum contrast ratio of 3:1.
Contrast requirements also apply to UI components such as input borders and focus indicators.

Elements.Title: Avoiding Color as the Sole Indicator
Elements.BodyText: Relying on color alone to convey information excludes users who are color blind or who use monochrome displays.
Elements.Notes: A classic example is a form validation that turns a field border red to indicate an error without providing a text message. Adding an icon and descriptive error text resolves this issue.

Items.Text: Color must always be supplemented by another visual cue such as shape, pattern, or text label.
Error states, status indicators, and data charts are common areas where color-only design fails.
Using redundant encoding ensures the information is available to all users regardless of color perception.

Elements.Title: Typography and Readability
Elements.BodyText: Font size, line spacing, and text layout directly affect the readability of interface content for users with cognitive or visual impairments.
Elements.Notes: WCAG 1.4.12 (Text Spacing) specifies that content must remain usable when line height is set to 1.5x font size, letter spacing to 0.12x, and paragraph spacing to 2x. Designers should test these overrides in prototypes.

Items.Text: Body text should be set at a minimum of 16px to support users with mild visual impairments.
Sufficient line height and paragraph spacing reduce cognitive load and support readability.
Avoid justified text alignment as it creates uneven spacing that can impede reading for dyslexic users.

Elements.Title: Focus Indicators and Visual State
Elements.BodyText: Visible focus indicators are essential for keyboard and switch-access users to understand which element is currently active on the screen.
Elements.Notes: WCAG 2.2 introduced Success Criterion 2.4.11 (Focus Appearance) with more specific requirements for focus indicator size and contrast. Many default browser focus rings are insufficient and should be custom designed.

Items.Text: Every interactive element must display a clearly visible focus state when activated via keyboard.
Focus indicators must meet contrast requirements relative to both the element and the surrounding background.
Designers should define custom focus styles rather than relying on default browser outlines.

Topics.Title: Keyboard Navigation and Motor Accessibility
Topics.Summary: This topic explores how interfaces must be designed to support full operation through keyboard input alone, serving users with motor disabilities and power users alike.

Elements.Title: Keyboard Operability Requirements
Elements.BodyText: Every interactive function in an interface must be reachable and operable using only a keyboard, without requiring specific timing or simultaneous key combinations.
Elements.Notes: This is codified in WCAG Success Criterion 2.1.1 (Keyboard). Exceptions exist for free-form drawing tools and similar inputs where the path of motion is essential.

Items.Text: All interactive elements including buttons, links, forms, and modals must be keyboard accessible.
Keyboard traps, where focus becomes stuck inside a component, are a critical failure and must be resolved.
Custom keyboard shortcuts should not conflict with existing browser or assistive technology shortcuts.

Elements.Title: Logical Tab Order and Focus Management
Elements.BodyText: The order in which keyboard focus moves through an interface must follow a logical, predictable sequence that reflects the visual and functional layout.
Elements.Notes: Tab order is determined by DOM order by default. Avoid using CSS to visually reorder elements in a way that diverges from DOM order, as this creates a confusing disconnect for keyboard users.

Items.Text: Tab order should follow a top-to-bottom, left-to-right sequence consistent with visual layout.
When modals or overlays open, focus must be programmatically moved to the new content.
When dialogs close, focus must return to the element that triggered the dialog.

Elements.Title: Skip Navigation Links
Elements.BodyText: Skip links allow keyboard users to bypass repetitive navigation blocks and jump directly to the main content of a page.
Elements.Notes: Skip links are typically the first focusable element on a page and may be visually hidden until focused. They are a Level A WCAG requirement under Success Criterion 2.4.1 (Bypass Blocks).

Items.Text: A skip to main content link must be provided as the first focusable element on each page.
Skip links may be visually hidden by default but must become visible when they receive keyboard focus.
Multiple skip links can be provided to allow users to jump to major sections such as navigation or search.

Elements.Title: Interaction Patterns for Custom Components
Elements.BodyText: Custom UI components such as carousels, dropdowns, and date pickers require explicit keyboard interaction patterns to be operable by keyboard users.
Elements.Notes: The ARIA Authoring Practices Guide (APG) published by W3C documents recommended keyboard patterns for common widgets. Students should consult this resource when designing custom components.

Items.Text: Custom components must implement keyboard interactions consistent with established design patterns.
Arrow keys are typically used for navigation within composite widgets such as menus and tab panels.
Escape should dismiss overlays and return focus to the triggering element in all custom components.

Topics.Title: Screen Reader Compatibility
Topics.Summary: This topic addresses how interfaces communicate meaning and structure to screen reader software, ensuring that users who are blind or have low vision receive an equivalent experience.

Elements.Title: Semantic HTML and Landmark Roles
Elements.BodyText: Using correct HTML elements and landmark roles provides screen readers with the structural context needed to interpret and navigate interface content.
Elements.Notes: Landmark roles such as banner, navigation, main, and contentinfo help screen reader users jump between page regions efficiently. Many of these are provided implicitly by native HTML5 elements like header, nav, main, and footer.

Items.Text: Native HTML elements such as button, nav, and heading tags convey built-in semantic meaning to assistive technologies.
Landmark regions allow screen reader users to navigate directly to major sections of a page.
Divs and spans carry no semantic meaning and should be supplemented with ARIA roles when used for interactive purposes.

Elements.Title: ARIA Labels and Descriptions
Elements.BodyText: ARIA attributes extend semantic meaning to custom components and provide additional context for screen reader users when native HTML semantics are insufficient.
Elements.Notes: The first rule of ARIA use is: do not use ARIA if a native HTML element can do the job. Overusing ARIA or applying it incorrectly can make interfaces less accessible rather than more.

Items.Text: aria-label provides an accessible name for an element that overrides its visible text label.
aria-describedby links an element to a longer descriptive string for additional context.
aria-labelledby associates an element with a visible heading or label elsewhere in the DOM.

Elements.Title: Image and Media Accessibility
Elements.BodyText: All non-text content must have a text alternative that conveys equivalent information to users who cannot perceive the visual or auditory content.
Elements.Notes: Decorative images should use an empty alt attribute (alt='') so screen readers skip them. Complex images such as charts should have extended descriptions either inline or linked nearby.

Items.Text: Informative images require descriptive alt text that communicates the image's meaning and purpose.
Decorative images must use an empty alt attribute to be ignored by screen readers.
Video content must include captions and, where appropriate, audio description tracks.

Elements.Title: Dynamic Content and Live Regions
Elements.BodyText: Content that updates dynamically on a page, such as status messages, alerts, or live data feeds, must be announced to screen reader users without requiring a page reload.
Elements.Notes: ARIA live regions with role='alert' or aria-live='polite' are used to announce dynamic updates. 'Assertive' announcements interrupt the user and should be reserved for urgent messages only.

Items.Text: ARIA live regions notify screen readers of content changes that occur without a full page reload.
Status messages such as form submission confirmations must be programmatically exposed to assistive technologies.
Use aria-live='polite' for non-urgent updates and aria-live='assertive' only for critical alerts.

Topics.Title: Inclusive Design Principles Beyond WCAG
Topics.Summary: This topic broadens the accessibility conversation to encompass inclusive design thinking, cognitive accessibility, and designing for the full spectrum of human diversity.

Elements.Title: The Social Model and Inclusive Design Mindset
Elements.BodyText: Inclusive design recognizes that disability is often created by environments and systems that fail to accommodate human diversity, rather than by individual impairment alone.
Elements.Notes: Microsoft's Inclusive Design Toolkit frames exclusion as a mismatch between a person and the environment. Designing for people with disabilities benefits all users — curb cuts help wheelchair users but also cyclists, parents with strollers, and delivery workers.

Items.Text: Inclusive design addresses the needs of people with permanent, temporary, and situational limitations.
Designing for edge cases typically improves the experience for the majority of users as well.
Accessibility should be treated as a design quality dimension, not a compliance afterthought.

Elements.Title: Cognitive Accessibility
Elements.BodyText: Designing for cognitive accessibility ensures that interfaces are understandable and usable by people with cognitive, learning, and neurological differences.
Elements.Notes: WCAG 2.2 and the forthcoming WCAG 3.0 place increasing emphasis on cognitive accessibility. Key considerations include reducing memory load, providing clear instructions, and avoiding timed interactions.

Items.Text: Use plain language, consistent navigation, and clear labeling to reduce cognitive load.
Avoid time limits on tasks, or provide users with the ability to extend or disable them.
Provide error prevention mechanisms such as input formatting hints and confirmation steps before irreversible actions.

Elements.Title: Responsive and Adaptive Design for Accessibility
Elements.BodyText: Interfaces must remain accessible across a range of screen sizes, orientations, input methods, and user-defined display settings.
Elements.Notes: WCAG 1.4.4 (Resize Text) requires that text can be resized up to 200% without loss of content or functionality. WCAG 1.3.4 (Orientation) prohibits restricting content to a single screen orientation unless essential.

Items.Text: Interfaces must support text resizing up to 200% without loss of content or functionality.
Content must be accessible in both portrait and landscape orientations.
Touch targets must be large enough to be operable by users with motor impairments, with a recommended minimum size of 44x44 pixels.

Elements.Title: Animation and Motion Sensitivity
Elements.BodyText: Excessive or unexpected motion in interfaces can cause discomfort or harm to users with vestibular disorders, epilepsy, or motion sensitivity.
Elements.Notes: WCAG 2.3.3 (Animation from Interactions) at Level AAA allows users to disable non-essential animation. The CSS prefers-reduced-motion media query enables designers to provide reduced-motion experiences automatically.

Items.Text: Provide users with a mechanism to pause, stop, or hide any animation that lasts more than five seconds.
Use the CSS prefers-reduced-motion media query to detect and respect user system preferences for reduced motion.
Avoid flashing content that exceeds three flashes per second to prevent risk of seizures.

Topics.Title: Accessibility Auditing
Topics.Summary: This topic covers the process of systematically evaluating an interface for accessibility failures and documenting findings to guide remediation.

Elements.Title: Audit Methods and Tools
Elements.BodyText: Accessibility auditing combines automated scanning tools with manual evaluation and assistive technology testing to surface a comprehensive set of accessibility issues.
Elements.Notes: Automated tools such as Axe, WAVE, and Lighthouse can detect approximately 30–40% of WCAG failures. The remaining issues require manual inspection and user testing. No single tool catches everything.

Items.Text: Automated accessibility scanners identify common issues such as missing alt text, low contrast, and missing form labels.
Manual testing with a keyboard alone is required to verify focus order, keyboard traps, and interaction patterns.
Testing with actual screen readers such as NVDA, JAWS, or VoiceOver is necessary to validate the assistive technology experience.

Elements.Title: Auditing Your Own Prototype
Elements.BodyText: Students will apply audit techniques directly to their own prototypes, using a structured checklist to evaluate each component against relevant WCAG success criteria.
Elements.Notes: Encourage students to use a WCAG quick reference or an audit checklist template. Common prototype issues include missing focus states, low contrast placeholder text, unlabeled icon buttons, and non-semantic custom components.

Items.Text: Begin the audit by reviewing the prototype with keyboard-only navigation to identify focus and operability issues.
Check all color combinations using a contrast analyzer tool against WCAG AA minimum thresholds.
Inspect all interactive elements to ensure they carry accessible names visible to assistive technologies.
Document each finding with its affected component, the relevant WCAG criterion, and a severity rating.

Elements.Title: Prioritizing Accessibility Findings
Elements.BodyText: Not all accessibility issues carry equal weight; findings must be ranked by severity and user impact to guide remediation efforts efficiently.
Elements.Notes: A common severity scale uses Critical, Serious, Moderate, and Minor ratings. Critical issues completely block access for some users and must be resolved before launch. Minor issues cause inconvenience but do not prevent task completion.

Items.Text: Critical issues prevent users from completing core tasks and must be resolved with highest priority.
Serious issues create significant barriers but may have workarounds; they should be addressed before launch.
Minor issues cause friction but do not block access and can be scheduled for iterative improvement.

Elements.Title: Writing Accessibility Findings and Recommendations
Elements.BodyText: Effective audit reports clearly describe each issue, its impact on users, the relevant guideline, and a concrete recommended fix.
Elements.Notes: Findings should be written in plain language that non-technical stakeholders can understand. Including screenshots with annotations and specific code or design recommendations accelerates remediation.

Items.Text: Each finding should identify the affected element, the WCAG criterion violated, and the observed failure.
Recommendations must be specific and actionable, describing exactly what change will resolve the issue.
Including the user impact statement helps stakeholders understand why the issue matters and prioritize accordingly.

Topics.Title: Applying Corrective Design Patterns
Topics.Summary: This topic focuses on translating audit findings into actionable design corrections, establishing accessible component patterns that can be reused across an interface.

Elements.Title: Designing Accessible Form Components
Elements.BodyText: Forms are among the most common sources of accessibility failures and require careful attention to labeling, error handling, and input structure.
Elements.Notes: Every form input must have a programmatically associated label, not just a visible placeholder. Placeholder text disappears on input and should not serve as the only label. Error messages must be associated with the relevant field using aria-describedby.

Items.Text: Every form input must have a persistently visible and programmatically associated label element.
Inline error messages must be specific, placed adjacent to the relevant field, and announced to screen readers.
Group related inputs such as radio buttons using fieldset and legend elements to provide context.

Elements.Title: Accessible Navigation Patterns
Elements.BodyText: Navigation components must be structured and coded so that all users can orient themselves within a site and move between sections efficiently.
Elements.Notes: Navigation landmarks should be labeled when multiple navigation regions exist on the same page to differentiate them for screen reader users. Breadcrumbs should be marked up with aria-label='Breadcrumb' and use aria-current='page' on the current item.

Items.Text: Primary navigation must be contained within a nav landmark element with a descriptive aria-label.
Active or current page links must be indicated programmatically using aria-current='page'.
Dropdown menus must be fully keyboard operable and follow established ARIA menu or disclosure patterns.

Elements.Title: Accessible Modals and Overlays
Elements.BodyText: Modal dialogs require careful focus management and ARIA implementation to ensure screen reader users understand the context and can interact with and dismiss the overlay.
Elements.Notes: When a modal opens, all content behind it should be made inert using the inert attribute or aria-hidden='true' so screen readers cannot accidentally navigate to background content. Focus must be trapped inside the modal while it is open.

Items.Text: Focus must move to the modal container or its first interactive element when the dialog opens.
Focus must be trapped within the modal so keyboard users cannot tab to background content.
The modal must be dismissible via the Escape key and focus must return to the triggering element on close.

Elements.Title: Accessible Data Visualization
Elements.BodyText: Charts, graphs, and other data visualizations must communicate their information through means beyond color and visual representation alone.
Elements.Notes: Providing a data table as an alternative to a chart satisfies both WCAG requirements and serves users who prefer tabular data. SVG-based charts can be made accessible using ARIA roles and titles embedded within the SVG.

Items.Text: All charts must include a text summary or accessible data table conveying the same information.
Color-coded data series must use additional differentiators such as patterns, shapes, or direct labels.
Interactive chart elements must be keyboard navigable and expose data values to screen readers.

Elements.Title: Iterating on Accessibility in Design Workflows
Elements.BodyText: Accessibility is most effectively integrated as a continuous practice throughout the design process rather than addressed only at the end through remediation.
Elements.Notes: Shifting accessibility left — addressing it during wireframing and component design rather than at QA — dramatically reduces the cost and effort of remediation. Design systems that encode accessible components by default make compliance scalable.

Items.Text: Accessibility criteria should be included in design requirements and acceptance criteria from project inception.
Reusable design system components should be built and tested for accessibility before being deployed across an interface.
Regular accessibility checkpoints during design reviews prevent issues from accumulating until late in development.
